By Pano Klironomos, Logan Roche, and Joseph Callaway

## Research Question

> Has energy usage or pricing significantly increased in places where data center buildout for AI is prevalent?

## **Trustworthiness/reputability**

The documentation available for the EIA-861M form is the dataset’s description as well as the corresponding survey. There are no missing entries/data but the dataset does start in 2010, and the data collected by the EIA before 2010 follows a different format missing many of the features of the newer dataset. The limitations in data quality for the form could be that companies could be intentionally misreporting what their energy usage is when they submit their mandatory report. For Joseph’s Washington D.C specific dataset, trustworthiness comes into question when you realize that these are submissions of individual companies rather than one source collecting several observations. Additionally there are rows in which reports are not formally submitted. There is a long stretch in which several properties’ data is unaccounted for. Another limitation is that the max year covered is 2025 so while still quite good it cannot extend into 2026\. Logan chose RECS 2020, which is one of the better-documented sources we could have picked. It comes from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, the federal statistical agency for energy, and it ships with a full codebook, technical documentation for both the housing and the consumption data, the actual survey forms, and a guide on using the survey weights correctly. The consumption numbers also aren't purely self-reported. Utilities were legally required to send in billing records, and EIA used those records to check and correct what households said. Still, there are real quality issues. The household survey only had about a 38.6% response rate. For electricity, around 14% of households had no billing data at all, so their usage was fully estimated from models. Propane and fuel oil coverage was only about 50%. Some survey answers were filled in by imputation, up to 22% for certain variables. On top of that, 2020 was a COVID year, with more people working from home, so the energy use in this data may not look like a normal year. Overall, Pano’s EIA government dataset seems most trustworthy and least biased for our research question.

## **Degree of relevance to research question**

For EIA-861M, The collection method is mandatory government reporting which means our conclusions can be trusted to not have bias. In order to answer our question, we will treat megawatt hours and energy prices in the commercial sector as a proxy for the increase in consumption by datacenters. If we could improve this source, we would like it to be more granular and see the commercial sector split into several types of commercial categories instead of aggregating it all together. Joseph’s Washington D.C dataset are the reports filed by companies annually to report on their energy consumption for each month of a year. The main proxy that would be relevant to our research question would be EnergyStar rating and electric use for each month column. It would help to have a year total column for electrical consumption because separating them between months would make visualization harder. Additionally if water consumption or natural gas emissions came into question, the monthly categories would prove useful. Logan’s dataset (RECS), on its own, can't answer our question. It has nothing about data centers, it only covers homes, and it's a single year, so it can't show whether anything "increased." Its value is timing. 2020 comes before the big AI buildout really took off, so RECS works as a pre-boom baseline for what households were using and paying, state by state. To use it we'd have to lean on proxies. State would stand in for "a place with heavy data center buildout," which is pretty coarse, since buildout is usually concentrated in a few counties or utility territories rather than a whole state. Dividing a household's total electricity cost by its total kWh would give a rough residential price, which is a stand-in for actual utility rates. If we could improve one thing, we'd add a later survey year (the 2024 RECS once its consumption data comes out) and finer geography like county or utility, so the data could actually line up with where data centers are being built. Pano’s dataset seems most relevant to the question because it covers all states and D.C and stretches back over 10 years, but the other datasets can be helpful to compare.

## **Ethical soundness**

For EIA-861M, there should be no possible bias because all states must report directly to the EIA, a government organization, each month. One ethical concern is that businesses that report for the commercial sector may be misreporting numbers. For the Washington D.C dataset, the biggest concern is the reports are made by the companies themselves under Washington DC’s benchmarking law. We foresee there being a potential issue with inaccurate numbers in this dataset as they are measured by people with the interests of their company in mind allowing room for bias. This might be interesting to cross examine with the total energy consumption per sector. Another potential ethical concern are the companies who choose to pay the fine of 30 cents per square foot to hide if they fail to file the report which could suggest those numbers being potentially hidden by the companies on purpose. The biggest bias risk for Logan’s RECS dataset is who responded. Response rates ranged from about 30% in New York to about 51% in Wisconsin, and the people who answer a 30-minute government survey may not look like the people who don't. Busy, lower-income, or non-English/Spanish-speaking households are especially likely to be undercounted. EIA weights the data to correct for this, but weighting can only fix differences it knows about. Logan’s survey also leaves out group quarters, vacant homes, and seasonal units, so some vulnerable groups aren't represented at all. On privacy, EIA does a good job. Addresses and local geography are removed and high values are top-coded, but that same protection is what keeps us from linking households to specific data center locations. The main ethical concern for our project is overclaiming. If we pair a 2020 baseline with later price data from other sources, it would be easy to blame data centers for higher bills when inflation, fuel prices, weather, and grid upgrades could just as easily explain the change.

## **Scope**

In EIA-861M, One row includes a breakdown of usage and sales in each sales sector per state each month. This represents the entire US population which is very relevant to the research question because we can compare and contrast states that have had larger or lesser datacenter buildouts. In the Washington D.C. dataset, one row represents a company’s annual power consumption report. This is exclusive to the Washington DC area and from 2012-2025. Ultimately it could serve as a good reference point for a subquestion of are companies lying about energy consumption. While it may not help solve the question as broadly as one of the other datasets it could potentially prove a useful resource. A claim that could be made about this particular set is after sorting by date and address, one may be able to notice how for there is one entry for each month for the latest year and how for subsequent years there are all zeros, this might be due to policy changes or that the number is cumulative but it is confusing. In the RECS dataset, one row is one household living in its primary home. The roughly 18,500 responding households are weighted to represent about 123.5 million occupied homes across all 50 states and DC. That's a strong national picture of residential energy use, but it misses the part of the grid where data centers actually live, the commercial and industrial sector. So the dataset can speak to how households might feel price effects, not to how much energy data centers themselves use. Claims someone could reasonably make with RECS include how electricity use and costs varied by state, region, or climate in 2020, how housing type and income relate to energy bills, and how common energy insecurity was. Claims they shouldn't make are anything about trends over time or about data centers specifically. That's why it fits best as supporting context alongside our team's main sources. All datasets have valuable observations and are all aggregated from different U.S. sectors that could provide insight into our research question. Overall, EIA-861M is the strongest dataset because it shows us historical electricity consumption across all states. RECS provides a very detailed look into residential energy use but lacks the time and sector coverage we need. The Washington D.C dataset provides more specific insights but cannot be used to look at the national level. By comparing the different collection methods and data scope, we can understand how they all have strengths and weaknesses toward answering our research question.
